The first four columns together make up what the chapter calls Physical Geography, which studies landforms, drainage, relief and slope in the lithosphere, composition, structure, weather, climate, winds and precipitation in the atmosphere, oceans, seas, lakes and rivers in the hydrosphere, and life forms, ecosystem, food chain and ecological balance in the biosphere.

The fifth column is Human Geography, which studies the relationship between man and his environment and the distribution of social and environmental phenomena around the world. The last column holds the techniques of the subject rather than its subject matter.

The chapter's own list of the skills of a geographer is:

- Observation
- Data collection using surveys, photographs and satellite images
- Land surveying with the help of instruments and advanced technology
- Data organisation
- Data interpretation
- Data representation with the help of graphs and maps
- Making maps
- Analysis with the help of statistical techniques
- Writing reports and presenting the findings

These skills are why the chapter calls Geography empirical and practical in nature. The study is scientific and is always supplemented with experiments, data, observation patterns, data analysis and research findings, rather than resting on theory alone.

The chapter adds one more skill that recent practice has made necessary: knowledge of computers, because mapping is now mostly done using GIS software and the use of GPS and GIS has become a mandatory aspect of geographical studies.

This pair states one of the dualisms of the subject: does nature rule us, or does man rule nature?

Some geographers hold that nature is more dominant than man, and the chapter calls that view environmental determinism. Others hold that man dominates nature, and that view is called possibilism.

Its importance is that the answer a geographer prefers shapes how they explain what they see. The existence of two such contrasting approaches side by side is what the chapter calls Dualism in Geography, and it is one of the things that makes Geography dualistic in nature.

This pair states a second dualism, about how a study should be organised. The chapter puts the choice as a question: shall we study various regions in which a sector is distributed, or study various sectors in a region?

A complete study of India takes one region and examines every sector within it. A study of only agriculture in India takes one sector and follows it across every region.

Its importance is that the two produce different kinds of knowledge from the same facts, and a geographer has to choose one of them before starting. Like environmental determinism and possibilism, the two approaches exist side by side, which is what the chapter means by Dualism in Geography.

The chapter supports these pairings directly. It says knowledge of Mathematics is essential for cartographic techniques and that drawing maps and diagrams requires it; that Geology, Meteorology, Hydrology and Pedology are linked with Geomorphology, Climatology, Oceanography and the Geography of Soils; and that Sociology, Political Science, Economics, History and Demography are closely linked with Social, Political, Economic, Population and Historical Geography respectively. Statistics, Psychology and Biology appear in the chapter's own diagram of the subject's links.

[Note: the chapter does not name Anthropology or Chemistry. Anthropology is entered for the row on racial structure and human evolution, and Chemistry for chemical weathering and acid rain, because no discipline the chapter does name covers them; both rows are inferred rather than taken from the text.]

Three of the seven entries are geography careers in the strict sense, because they ask for a geography qualification by name.

Entry 1, the UPSC Class-1 Officer post with the National Atlas of Thematic Mapping organisation of India, asks for M.A./M.Sc. Geography, a cartographer or a Masters in Urban Planning. The chapter lists Cartographer as a career with a specialisation in Cartography and G.I.S.

Entry 2, the Urban planner with the Mumbai Mahanagar Palika, asks for MA Geography among its qualifications. The chapter lists Urban Planner as a career with a specialisation in Urban Geography.

Entry 3, the Assistant professor post, names Geography among its subjects and asks for graduation and post graduation in it with NET/SET. This is the teaching career the chapter mentions when it says teaching is a field that needs people from a Geography background.

Entry 4, the UN internship, asks for a Masters in Development Studies, Gender Studies or Social Sciences. A geographer may qualify through the Social Sciences route, but the post does not ask for Geography, so it is open to a geographer rather than a geography career.

Entries 6 and 7, the Bank PO exam and the UPSC Combined Defence Services, are open to any graduate, so a geographer may apply but the subject gives no particular advantage. The chapter does note that Geography provides a good base of knowledge in competitive examinations.

Entry 5, the UPSC Engineering Services Examination, is open only to engineering graduates and is not available to a geographer at all.

Because the things Human Geography studies are the subject matter of several other disciplines at the same time, and it studies them for their spatial attributes.

The chapter states that in the case of Human Geography, every social science studied separately has an interface with a branch of Human Geography because of their spatial attributes. It names the pairings: Sociology, Political Science, Economics, History and Demography are closely linked with Social, Political, Economic, Population and Historical Geography respectively.

So a question about voting patterns belongs to Political Science and to Political Geography at once, and a question about incomes and resources belongs to Economics and to Economic Geography at once. Human Geography adds the question of where, which the parent discipline does not ask. This is why the chapter concludes that Geography has a strong interface with the natural as well as the social sciences, and calls it an integrating and interdisciplinary discipline.

Because the phenomena it studies are not static, and the subject itself keeps changing with them.

The chapter states that geographical phenomena, whether physical or human, are highly dynamic and change over time. Weather is studied over roughly thirty years before the climate of a place is decided; the population of India or of the world, the development of a landform and the age of the earth are all phenomena studied through time. Because Geography is a study of space and of time together, it cannot be fixed.

The subject is dynamic in a second sense too. The chapter says its dynamic nature keeps adding new things to it: audio-visual media and Information Technology have enriched its database, GPS and GIS have become mandatory, and mathematical and computer models are increasingly used in Applied Geography.

Because two contrasting approaches to the same questions exist side by side within it, and the subject has not replaced one with the other.

The chapter defines Dualism in Geography as the existence of two contrasting or separate approaches, and gives two examples. On the relation between man and nature, some geographers hold that nature is more dominant than man, which is environmental determinism, while others hold that man dominates nature, which is possibilism. On how a study should be organised, a geographer must choose between studying the various regions in which a sector is distributed and studying the various sectors within one region.

The chapter adds that there are many other such dualistic approaches in Geography, and that this is what makes Geography dualistic in nature.

Physical Geography studies the earth's physical environment, and each part of that environment is also the subject of a separate science, so the two run alongside each other.

The chapter gives the pairings directly: Geology, Meteorology, Hydrology and Pedology are linked with the fields of Physical Geography known as Geomorphology, Climatology, Oceanography and the Geography of Soils respectively.

The link runs through subject matter. Physical Geography includes landforms, drainage, relief and slope in the lithosphere; composition, structure, weather, climate, winds, precipitation and climate types in the atmosphere; oceans, seas, lakes and rivers in the hydrosphere; and life forms, ecosystem, food chain and ecological balance in the biosphere. Every one of those is studied by a natural science as well.

What Physical Geography adds is the spatial question. It asks where these things occur, how they are distributed and why, whereas the parent science asks what they are and how they work.

The chapter divides the subject matter of Geography into two major themes, physical factors and human factors, and these have given rise to the two main branches.

Physical Geography includes the study of landforms, drainage, relief and slope, which belong to the lithosphere; composition, structure, weather and climate, winds, precipitation and climate types, which belong to the atmosphere; oceans, seas, lakes and rivers, which belong to the hydrosphere; and life forms including human beings and macro-organisms, ecosystem, food chain and ecological balance, which belong to the biosphere. Its named fields include Geomorphology, Climatology, Oceanography and the Geography of Soils.

Human Geography studies the relationship between man and his environment and the distribution of the various social and environmental phenomena related to humans around the world. Its named branches include Social, Political, Economic, Population and Historical Geography.

Alongside these sit the technique branches, which the chapter groups as Geographic Techniques: Cartography, Geographic Information Systems, Remote Sensing and quantification methods.

The chapter notes that branches keep appearing, because the skills of the geographer enrich the subject and newer branches of geography keep developing with time.

The chapter describes the recent direction of the subject as a move from description towards prediction, driven by technology.

A geographer explains phenomena in a frame of cause and effect, which helps in analysis but also allows the future to be predicted through data collection and modelling. This opens intra-disciplinary and inter-disciplinary avenues and widens the scope of the subject.

Technology has changed the working methods. Audio-visual media and Information Technology have enriched the database. Computers and software have improved data collection, interpretation, analysis and presentation. The use of GPS and GIS has become a mandatory aspect of geographical studies, and mapping is now mostly done using GIS software, so knowledge of computers is an added skill a geographer now requires. The use of apps has further extended the subject's applications in daily life.

Mathematical modelling and computer models are increasingly used in Applied Geography, to predict the future growth and density of population, land use, intensity of cropping, migration, patterns of population, industrialisation, urbanisation and the growth of cities and slums. The same models are used to forecast weather, climate change, change in sea level, environmental pollution, soil erosion, forest depletion and the evolution of landforms.

The chapter closes the theme by noting that Geography is emerging as a discipline for evaluating and managing natural resources, and that the Sustainable Development Goals given by the United Nations are related to various aspects of Geography.

The chapter lists the skills of a geographer as observation; data collection using surveys, photographs and satellite images; land surveying with the help of instruments and advanced technology; data organisation; data interpretation; data representation with the help of graphs and maps; making maps; analysis with the help of statistical techniques; and writing reports and presenting the findings.

These skills are what make the subject empirical and practical in nature. The study is scientific and is always supplemented with experiments, data, observation patterns, data analysis and research findings, rather than resting on theory. It is supported by evidence gathered and analysed through various tools and techniques.

The chapter points out that the subject began with these skills. Geography developed through observations, and earlier scholars wrote a great deal describing the earth. It also notes that the skills keep growing: knowledge of computers is now an added skill, because mapping is mostly done using GIS software and the use of GPS and GIS has become mandatory.

Geography is useful in daily life because it explains where things are, why they are there, and what will happen to them next, and the chapter gives several examples of each.

It explains the places we live in and use. The chapter notes that a geographer studies the crops grown in different regions and understands them as a result of different climates, soils, market demand and the application of technology, and that by studying a region he can say which economic activities are most suitable for it. That is the knowledge behind a farmer's choice of crop and a planner's choice of site.

It is used to anticipate what is coming. The chapter says mathematical and computer models are used to predict the future growth and density of population, land use, intensity of cropping, migration, industrialisation, urbanisation and the growth of cities and slums, and to forecast weather, climate change, change in sea level, environmental pollution, soil erosion and forest depletion. Weather forecasting alone is something people use every day.

It reaches daily life through technology. The chapter notes that the use of GPS and GIS has become a mandatory aspect of geographical studies, that mapping is now mostly done using GIS software, and that the use of apps has further enhanced the subject's applications in daily life. Every navigation app rests on this.

It is needed for the way we use resources. The chapter says Geography is emerging as a discipline of evaluating and managing natural resources, that the accelerated pace of resource utilisation has created ecological imbalance in the world, and that a better understanding of Geography is absolutely essential for sustainable development and for avoiding clashes between man and nature. The Sustainable Development Goals given by the United Nations are related to various aspects of Geography.

Finally, it is useful as a livelihood. The chapter lists careers from cartographer and climatologist to urban planner, demographer, disaster management specialist and data scientist, and notes that Geography provides a good base of knowledge in competitive examinations.

The chapter states that almost every discipline, under the natural as well as the social sciences, is linked with Geography, and it sets out the links branch by branch.

With the natural sciences, the link runs through Physical Geography. Geology, Meteorology, Hydrology and Pedology are linked with Geomorphology, Climatology, Oceanography and the Geography of Soils respectively. Biology meets the subject through Biogeography, in the study of biomes, food chains and forests.

With Mathematics and Statistics, the link runs through technique. Knowledge of Mathematics is essential for cartographic techniques, and drawing maps and diagrams requires an understanding of it. For data analysis geographers use various statistical techniques and hypothesis testing.

With the social sciences, the link runs through Human Geography. The chapter says every social science studied separately has an interface with a branch of Human Geography because of their spatial attributes, and names the pairings: Sociology, Political Science, Economics, History and Demography are closely linked with Social, Political, Economic, Population and Historical Geography respectively.

Computer Science has joined this list recently, through Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing.

The chapter draws two conclusions from all this. Geography has a strong interface with the natural as well as the social sciences; and at the same time every sub-discipline in Geography has its own scope, because its subject matter varies over space and time. Geography has adopted and developed a great deal from other disciplines within its own boundaries, and many of its branches have grown out of mainstream disciplines, which is what makes it an integrating and interdisciplinary discipline.

The chapter describes the nature of Geography under four heads.

It is a study of space and time. Geography studies the earth and the phenomena related to it. The earth is dynamic, and there are variations in its physical and cultural environments; geographers study these distributions and patterns, and also the causes behind them, so a geographer is interested in the cause and effect relationship between them. He studies space, or area, or a geographical location. The phenomena are not static but highly dynamic and change over time, so weather is studied over roughly thirty years before the climate of a place is decided. In short, a geographer tries to answer the questions where, when, what and why.

It is dynamic. Because it studies both space and time, and because technology keeps adding new methods and new data, the subject does not stand still.

It is empirical and practical. The skills required to study Geography, and the methods and techniques used in it, make it so. The study is very scientific and is always supplemented with experiments, data, observation patterns, data analysis and research findings, rather than resting on theory. Historically the subject developed through observation: the chapter cites the Greek scholar Hecataeus, whose book Ges-Periodus was published most probably before the end of the 6th century BC and gives the first systematic description of the world, Ptolemy's Geography with its atlas, and Strabo's Geographica, an encyclopaedia of geographical knowledge in seventeen volumes.

It is dualistic. Two contrasting approaches exist side by side, which the chapter calls Dualism in Geography: environmental determinism against possibilism, and the study of regions against the study of sectors.

To these the chapter adds that Geography is an integrating and interdisciplinary discipline, since almost every natural and social science is linked with it and many of its branches have developed out of mainstream disciplines.

| Point of difference | Physical Geography | Human Geography |
|---|---|---|
| Theme it belongs to | The physical factors in the subject matter of Geography | The human factors in the subject matter of Geography |
| What it studies | The physical environment of the earth | The relationship between man and his environment, and the distribution of social and environmental phenomena related to humans |
| Lithosphere and atmosphere content | Landforms, drainage, relief, slope; composition, structure, weather and climate, winds, precipitation, climate types | Not its subject matter |
| Hydrosphere and biosphere content | Oceans, seas, lakes, rivers; life forms including human beings and macro-organisms, ecosystem, food chain, ecological balance | Not its subject matter |
| Named branches | Geomorphology, Climatology, Oceanography, Geography of Soils | Social, Political, Economic, Population and Historical Geography |
| Disciplines it interfaces with | Geology, Meteorology, Hydrology, Pedology | Sociology, Political Science, Economics, History, Demography |

| Point of difference | Possibilism | Determinism |
|---|---|---|
| Core belief | Man dominates nature | Nature is more dominant than man |
| Full name used in the chapter | Possibilism | Environmental determinism |
| Who is active | Man, who chooses among the possibilities nature offers | Nature, which sets what man can do |
| Answer to 'does nature rule us or does man rule nature?' | Man rules nature | Nature rules us |

The two are not separate subjects but two contrasting views held within the same one. The chapter presents them as its leading example of Dualism in Geography, the existence of two contrasting or separate approaches side by side, and says this is part of what makes Geography dualistic in nature.

Draw GEOGRAPHY at the centre of the diagram. From it take three main arms, and label the disciplines that each arm connects to.

Arm 1, Physical Geography. Show its fields as Geomorphology, Climatology, Biogeography and the Geography of Soils, and against them place the linked disciplines Geology, Meteorology, Biology and Pedology. Engineering may be shown on this arm as well.

Arm 2, Human Geography. Show its branches as Social, Political, Economic, Population, Behavioral and Historical Geography, and against them place the linked disciplines Sociology, Political Science, Economics, Demography, Psychology and History.

Arm 3, Geographic Techniques. Show Cartography, Geographic Information Systems, Remote Sensing, Geodesy and Quantification Methods in Geography, and against them place the linked disciplines Statistics and Computer Science.

Label every box, and draw the connecting lines from the central GEOGRAPHY box outwards so that each discipline is joined to the branch it supports. Title the diagram 'Relationship of Geography with other subjects'.

Draw a central box labelled SKILLS OF A GEOGRAPHER, and take one labelled arm out to each skill.

The skills to label are: Observation; Data collection using surveys, photographs and satellite images; Land surveying with the help of instruments and advanced technology; Data organisation; Data interpretation; Data representation with the help of graphs and maps; Making maps; Analysis with the help of statistical techniques; and Writing reports and presenting the findings.

It helps to arrange them in working order round the centre, since that is the order in which a geographer uses them: observe, collect and survey, organise, interpret and analyse, represent and map, and finally report.

Knowledge of computers may be added as a further skill, because the chapter notes that mapping is now mostly done using GIS software and that the use of GPS and GIS has become a mandatory aspect of geographical studies.
